title: The Accidental Se: Mishaps Without Blame

sections.content: You know pronoun combinations with *se* from A2 Unit 25. New here is the **accidental *se*** construction: *se* + indirect object pronoun (*me, te, le, nos, les*) + 3rd-person verb. Spanish uses it for everyday mishaps — forgetting, dropping, spilling, burning, spoiling — to present the event as unintentional rather than deliberate: *Se me olvidaron las llaves*, *Se le cayó la bandeja*, *Se nos quemó el arroz*. Notice two essential rules: *se* always comes first before *me / te / le / nos / les*, and the verb agrees with the **thing** that was dropped or forgotten, not with the person (*Se me rompió el vaso* vs *Se me rompieron los vasos*).

sections.title: Structure of accidental se
rows: *Se me derramó el caldo* ('I accidentally spilled the broth').
*Se te olvidaron las llaves* ('You accidentally forgot the keys').
*Se* ALWAYS precedes *me / te / le / nos / les* (*Se nos echó a perder la comida*, never *Nos se…*).

items.spanish: Por un despiste, se me quemó la salsa mientras atendía la puerta.
items.english: Through a lapse of attention, I accidentally burned the sauce while answering the door.

items.spanish: Se le derramó el caldo caliente sobre el mantel limpio.
items.english: He accidentally spilled the hot broth onto the clean tablecloth.

items.spanish: Se nos olvidaron las llaves dentro del apartamento al salir con prisa.
items.english: We accidentally left the keys inside the apartment when leaving in a hurry.

items.spanish: Se les cayó la bandeja justo antes de llegar a la mesa.
items.english: They accidentally dropped the tray just before reaching the table.

sections.content: English makes the person the subject (*I dropped the keys*, *I forgot my glasses*), so learners often conjugate the verb for the person (*Se me olvidé las llaves* — wrong). Match the verb to the object: *las llaves* is plural, so *se me olvidaron*.
